name: Methi Thepla
cuisine: Gujarati (spiced whole-wheat flatbread with fresh fenugreek leaves; classic Gujarati breakfast, tiffin and travel food)

ingredients.name: Groundnut oil (or any neutral oil)
ingredients.householdMeasure: 1 tsp in the dough + about 1½ tsp for cooking

ingredients.name: Green chilli (hari mirch)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ chilli, very finely chopped or crushed

equipment: Mixing bowl (a wide bowl or a plate with a rim, called a "parat")
Knife and chopping board for the methi
Colander or sieve to wash and drain methi (or a bowl and your hands)
Small bowl and spoon for the cooking oil
Clean cotton cloth or a roti box to keep cooked theplas soft; for travel, paper towel and a steel or foil container
Measuring spoons and a ½-cup measure (normal kitchen spoons are fine)

steps.title: Pick the methi leaves
steps.text: Pull the leaves off the stems of the methi bunch until you have about 30 g of leaves (about 1 loosely packed cup before chopping). Throw away thick stems and yellow leaves.
steps.tip: Thick stems taste bitter and poke through the thepla when you roll it.
steps.visualCue: A heap of only green leaves and very tender tips; no hard stems.
steps.cameraCheck: The picked leaves in a bowl
steps.videoShot: Fingers pinching methi leaves off the stems into a bowl.

steps.title: Wash the leaves
steps.text: Put them in a bowl of water, swish, lift them out into a colander and repeat 2 times, until no grit settles at the bottom.
steps.visualCue: Clear water, no sand at the bottom of the bowl.
steps.videoShot: Methi leaves being lifted out of water into a colander.

steps.title: Drain and chop
steps.text: Shake off the water, pat the leaves dry in a towel, and chop them finely.
steps.tip: Dry leaves matter. Wet leaves release extra water and make the dough sticky.
steps.visualCue: Small, even pieces; the leaves are damp, not dripping.
steps.cameraCheck: The chopped methi on the board
steps.videoShot: A knife chopping a pile of methi leaves.

steps.title: Add the flours to the bowl
steps.text: Put 60 g (½ cup) whole wheat flour and 10 g (1 heaped tbsp) besan in the mixing bowl.
steps.visualCue: Two small heaps, brown and pale yellow.
steps.videoShot: Atta and besan being spooned into a bowl.

steps.title: Add the spices
steps.text: Add ⅛ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp red chilli powder, ½ tsp coriander powder, ¼ tsp ajwain (crush it between your palms as you add it), ½ tsp sesame seeds, ½ tsp sugar and ¼ tsp salt.
steps.visualCue: Colourful spice heaps on the flour.
steps.videoShot: Ajwain being rubbed between palms over the bowl.

steps.title: Add the methi, ginger and chilli
steps.text: Add the chopped methi, ½ tsp grated ginger and the finely chopped green chilli.
steps.visualCue: Green leaves on top of the spiced flour.
steps.videoShot: Chopped methi tipped into the bowl.

steps.title: Add the oil and mix
steps.text: Add 1 tsp oil and rub everything together with your fingertips for 1 minute.
steps.visualCue: The flour turns evenly yellow-green and looks like damp crumbs; the methi starts to wilt slightly.
steps.videoShot: Fingers rubbing oil, flour and methi together.

steps.title: Add the curd and knead
steps.text: Add 1½ tbsp (25 g) curd and knead. Add water only 1 tsp at a time, and only if the dough is still dry and cracking after 1 minute of kneading.
steps.tip: Go slow with water. The salt draws water out of the methi while the dough rests, so a dough that is too soft now becomes sticky later. Little water also means longer shelf life.
steps.visualCue: A soft, smooth, non-sticky dough, slightly firmer than chapati dough; it doesn't stick to your fingers.
steps.videoShot: Hands kneading a green-flecked dough in the bowl.

steps.title: Rest the dough
steps.text: Smear a few drops of oil on the dough ball, cover the bowl with a plate and leave it.
steps.visualCue: The dough feels a little softer and more elastic after resting.
steps.videoShot: A plate placed over the dough bowl.

steps.title: Divide the dough
steps.text: Knead the dough for 20 seconds and divide it into 3 equal balls (about 45 g each). Roll each ball smooth between your palms and flatten it slightly.
steps.visualCue: 3 smooth, crack-free balls the size of a large lemon.
steps.videoShot: Dough pinched into 3 balls and rolled between palms.

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Put the tawa on medium heat.
steps.visualCue: A drop of water sizzles and disappears in 2–3 seconds.
steps.videoShot: A water drop sizzling on the hot tawa.

steps.title: Roll the first thepla
steps.text: Dip one ball in the dusting flour and roll it into a thin round of about 15–16 cm (6 inch), about 2 mm thick, dusting lightly if it sticks.
steps.tip: Theplas are thinner than parathas and are not folded. Shape doesn't matter; even thickness does, so all parts cook at the same time.
steps.visualCue: An even, thin round; you can see the green methi flecks through it.
steps.cameraCheck: The rolled thepla on the board
steps.videoShot: A rolling pin rolling out a green-flecked round.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Lay the thepla on the hot tawa.
steps.visualCue: Small bubbles appear on top and the underside gets light spots.
steps.videoShot: The thepla laid on the tawa, bubbles rising.

steps.title: Flip it
steps.text: Turn the thepla over with the spatula.
steps.visualCue: The cooked side shows light brown spots.
steps.videoShot: The spatula flipping the thepla.

steps.title: Oil the top
steps.text: Spread about ¼ tsp oil over the top of the thepla with the back of a spoon.
steps.visualCue: A thin, even sheen of oil.
steps.videoShot: A spoon spreading oil in circles on the thepla.

steps.title: Flip and oil the other side
steps.text: Flip again, spread another ¼ tsp oil on the new top side, and press gently with the spatula.
steps.visualCue: The thepla puffs in places and sizzles.
steps.videoShot: The spatula pressing the edges of the sizzling thepla.

steps.title: Finish cooking
steps.text: Flip 1–2 more times, pressing the edges, until both sides have golden-brown spots and there are no pale, damp-looking patches.
steps.tip: Cooking fully matters for travel. Pale damp patches mean leftover moisture, and those spoil first.
steps.visualCue: Golden-brown spots on both sides, slightly crisp edges, a toasty methi smell.
steps.cameraCheck: Both sides of the cooked thepla
steps.videoShot: A golden-spotted thepla being flipped.

steps.title: Keep it warm
steps.text: Move the thepla to a plate lined with a cotton cloth or into a roti box and cover it.
steps.visualCue: The thepla is wrapped and steam stays inside.
steps.videoShot: The thepla folded into a cloth.

steps.title: Repeat for the other 2 theplas
steps.text: Roll, cook and oil the other 2 balls the same way (steps 12–18), rolling the next one while the current one cooks.
steps.visualCue: A stack of 3 golden-spotted theplas.
steps.videoShot: The third thepla added to the stack.

steps.title: Serve, or cool for travel
steps.text: Serve warm with curd and pickle. For a tiffin or travel, spread them on a plate or rack (not stacked) until completely cool, then stack them with a paper towel between them and close the box.
steps.tip: Packing warm theplas traps steam, which makes them soggy and shortens their shelf life.
steps.visualCue: For travel, the theplas feel cool to the touch, with no steam or condensation.
steps.cameraCheck: The 3 theplas on a plate (or the packed box)
steps.videoShot: Theplas folded in quarters beside a bowl of curd and a spoon of chhundo.

reasons: whole wheat flour plus besan and fresh methi give about 9 g fibre, useful iron, magnesium and folate, and about 12 g protein, and the theplas are tawa-roasted, not fried, with mostly unsaturated oil. Points off for a fairly high oil load (12 ml) for a bread, sodium just over 30% before any pickle, and protein that is moderate unless you add curd. Sellers often cook with more oil or ghee and serve sweet chhundo or salty pickle; some advertise "zero maida", which suggests maida is sometimes mixed in elsewhere.

researchRating.basis: methi thepla is described as the most popular kind of thepla and a signature Gujarati breakfast and travel food. It has dedicated recipes on nearly every major Indian recipe site (Veg Recipes of India, Indian Healthy Recipes, Hebbar's Kitchen, Tarla Dalal with a video, Maayeka, Raks Kitchen, My Food Story), Swiggy's own food blog lists it among must-try Gujarati dishes, and Mumbai has restaurants built around it (Thepla Junction with about 25 types; Thepla House by Tejal's Kitchen). Deduction because fresh methi is bitter for some people and picking the leaves is slow. Recipe-card vote counts were not collected in this run (search budget ran out), so the rating rests on how widely the dish is covered and praised rather than on star averages.

storage: Room temperature: about 2 days (up to 3 in cool, dry weather) in a closed steel box or wrapped in foil, after cooling completely. Theplas last well because they are kneaded with curd and oil and very little water and are cooked dry. In hot, humid Mumbai weather, plan to eat them within 1–2 days or keep them chilled. Fridge: 5–7 days in an airtight box or zip bag, with paper between layers. Freezer: 1–2 months, separated with baking paper, in a zip bag. Reheat: warm on a hot tawa for 20–30 seconds a side (from frozen, 1 min a side), or microwave 2–3 together under a damp paper towel for 15–20 seconds. They are fine eaten cold. Signs to discard: a sour or musty smell, slimy feel or any spots of mould.
leftoverRemix: Thepla khakhra chips with a dip. Cut 1–2 day old theplas into triangles and roast them on a tawa on low heat, pressing with a folded cloth, for 3–4 min a side until crisp like khakhra (or bake at 160 °C for 10–12 min). Serve with hung curd mixed with roasted cumin, chilli flakes and coriander. Or make a thepla wrap: spread green chutney on a thepla, fill it with paneer bhurji or leftover sabzi and roll it up.
burnOff: about 5.7 km of running (400 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 8 km of brisk walking (about 1 h 35 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.). This is for the theplas alone; 100 g curd adds about 1 km of running, and 1 tbsp chhundo about 0.8 km.

navratri.reason: whole wheat flour and besan are grains/pulses avoided on vrat (assumption: common North and West Indian vrat rules; rajgira or singhara theplas are the vrat alternative, not this dish)

ekadashi.reason: wheat and other grains and pulses are avoided on Ekadashi

jain.reason: swap fresh ginger for dry ginger powder (sonth); note that many observant Jains also avoid green leafy vegetables like methi on certain tithi days and during Paryushan, so check family practice

ramadan.reason: a filling, slow-digesting whole-wheat flatbread for sehri that keeps well; eat it with curd for protein and keep pickle small, as it adds salt before a long fast

jain.reason: replace fresh ginger (a root) with ¼ tsp dry ginger powder (sonth); everything else is Jain-friendly, and a "Jain Methi Thepla" is sold in Mumbai (see Jain variant)

vegan.reason: the dough uses 25 g curd; knead with water and ½ tsp lemon juice instead (see Vegan variant)

pescatarian.reason: contains no meat or poultry; a vegetarian dish fits a pescatarian diet

sattvik.reason: this recipe uses no onion or garlic (some families add garlic paste; leave it out)

glutenFree.reason: made with whole wheat flour (atta); hing, if added, is usually compounded with wheat flour too (see Gluten-free variant: bajra methi dhebra)

dairyFree.reason: curd in the dough; same swap as the Vegan variant, and cook with oil, not ghee or butter

description: A vegetarian, sattvik (no onion, no garlic) Gujarati fenugreek flatbread that travels well; Jain, vegan, dairy-free, gluten-free bajra and low-oil versions below.
